049.name: Imperial Exams
049.hitokoto: A test that ran for 1,300 years stopped with a single edict, on 2 September 1905.
body: The exams are held to begin in 598, when Emperor Wen of Sui decreed that men be raised up in two categories, the upright and disciplined and the pure and capable. Choosing officials by examination result rather than by birth was exceptional for its time, and for the 1,300 years that followed, reading books and entering office was the surest road to advancement in East Asia. In the Tang, the jinshi category passed 1 or 2 per cent of some 1,000 candidates, about 30 men a year.

On 31 August 1905, Yuan Shikai, Viceroy of Zhili, and Zhang Zhidong, Viceroy of Huguang, with others, submitted the Memorial Requesting the Immediate Halt of the Imperial Exams and the Extension of Schools, arguing that while the exams stood even one day longer, scholars would keep hoping to pass by luck and turn away from practical learning. On 2 September (4th day of the 8th month of Guangxu 31) the Cabinet promulgated an imperial edict ordering that from the bingwu session all provincial and metropolitan examinations be halted uniformly, and the annual and sessional examinations in each province stop at once.

The last exam held was the jiachen grace session of 1904, and its first graduate was Liu Chunlin of Suning in Zhili. On his sixtieth birthday he wrote of himself as the last of the first men. The arrangement by which one examination settles a life did not disappear, however: the national university entrance examination begun in 1952 is called the imperial exam of our day. Discontinued, and back in stock 47 years later.

made.label: 598 The decree of two categories
made.fact: In 598 (Kaihuang 18), Emperor Wen of Sui (Yang Jian) decreed that capital officials of the fifth rank and above, together with the area commanders and prefects, were to raise up men in two categories, "upright and disciplined" and "pure and capable". This is held to be the start of choosing officials by examination result rather than by birth. On another view the start is Emperor Yang's creation of the jinshi category in the Daye era (605 or 607).

discontinued.label: 1905 The edict halting the exams
discontinued.fact: On the 4th day of the 8th month of Guangxu 31 (2 September 1905) the Cabinet promulgated an imperial edict ordering that "from the bingwu session, all provincial and metropolitan examinations are to be halted uniformly, and the annual and sessional examinations in each province are also to stop at once". It followed the Memorial Requesting the Immediate Halt of the Imperial Exams and the Extension of Schools, submitted by Yuan Shikai and others the day before.

restocked.label: 1952 Gaokao
restocked.fact: On 15 August 1952 the national unified university entrance examination (the National Unified Examination for Admissions to General Universities and Colleges) began, and it is still called "the imperial exam of our day".

keyfacts.text: On 31 August 1905, Yuan Shikai, Viceroy of Zhili, Zhang Zhidong, Viceroy of Huguang, and others submitted the Memorial Requesting the Immediate Halt of the Imperial Exams and the Extension of Schools, calling for abolition at once: "while the exams are not stopped for a single day, scholars all keep a mind to pass by luck, and it divides their will to grind at solid learning."

The edict of abolition is dated the 4th day of the 8th month of Guangxu 31 (2 September 1905) and ordered that "from the bingwu session, all provincial and metropolitan examinations are to be halted uniformly, and the annual and sessional examinations in each province are also to stop at once; as for the juren, gongsheng and shengyuan of earlier years, ways forward are to be given them, each according to his case". The bingwu session fell in 1906.

The last exam actually held was the jiachen grace session of 1904 (Guangxu 30), a grace session set up for the seventieth birthday of the Empress Dowager Cixi. Its first graduate was Liu Chunlin (1872-1942) of Suning in Zhili, known as the last zhuangyuan in China.
The jinshi category, the most important in the Tang, passed 1 to 2 per cent of some 1,000 candidates, about 30 men a year. The average age of final successful candidates is put at around 36.

The eight-legged essay was abolished first, in 1902 (Guangxu 28), and the exams themselves three years later. Before abolition, a policy of reducing the numbers passing the provincial and metropolitan examinations over three successive sessions had already been settled in a memorial from the ministers of education.

The examinations of the Korean dynasty were abolished eleven years earlier, in 1894, by a resolution of the Deliberative Council ("abolish the examination system, establish a new method of appointing officials").

050.name: Duel (code of honour)
050.hitokoto: More than eleven bans were piled up, and honour was still paid in blood for 300 years.
body: The rules of the duel were first set down in writing in Renaissance Italy, and France raised them into a code of honour on a national scale. A nobleman who had been insulted named seconds, demanded satisfaction and settled the matter with the sword. Going to court was taken as proof of cowardice: honour was restored by one's own blood, not in a courtroom. Contemporary estimates put the dead under Henry IV at several thousand a year.

The crown treated this as an infringement of royal prerogative. On 2 June 1626 Louis XIII set the death penalty for a duel fought with seconds, and the next year he had François de Montmorency-Bouteville executed for duelling in broad daylight on the Place Royale in Paris. Louis XIV piled up more than eleven edicts of prohibition between 1643 and 1711. French officers still fought about 10,000 duels between 1685 and 1716, and more than 400 of them died.

The bans worked differently from country to country. In England fatal duels ended with a single case in 1852; Prussia forbade duelling in 1851. Russia went the other way: a law of 1894 left the question of whether a duel should be fought to a court of honour of the officer corps. The country that forbade and the country that allowed had changed places. The last duel of honour in France was fought on 21 April 1967, with swords, between two sitting members of parliament.

made.label: 16th c. A code of honour
made.fact: The written codification of duelling practice (code duello) began in Renaissance Italy, and France shaped it into a code of honour on a national scale. A nobleman who had been insulted named seconds, demanded satisfaction of his opponent and settled the matter with the sword. Contemporary estimates of deaths by duel from the reign of Henry II to that of Henry IV run to 6,000 (Henry II) and 8,000 (Henry IV), with 2,000 in 1606 and 4,000 in 1607, figures said to exceed the dead of the wars of religion. These are contemporary estimates, with no confirmation of the actual numbers.

discontinued.label: 1626 Louis XIII's edict
discontinued.fact: On 2 June 1626 an edict of Louis XIII, driven by Richelieu, set the death penalty for a duel fought with seconds and the loss of titles and pensions for an armed confrontation. Richelieu had himself lost a brother in a duel. On 21 June the following year, François de Montmorency-Bouteville, who had deliberately duelled in broad daylight on the Place Royale in Paris, was actually executed.

keyfacts.text: The edict of Louis XIII of 2 June 1626 set the death penalty for a duel fought with seconds, and the loss of titles and pensions for an armed confrontation. Bouteville was executed on 21 June 1627.

Between June 1643 and October 1711 Louis XIV issued more than eleven edicts against duelling, treating a duel as equivalent to an infringement of royal prerogative (lèse-majesté). French officers still fought about 10,000 duels between 1685 and 1716, with more than 400 dead.
The last duel in England to leave a man dead was in 1852, near Englefield Green, between two exiled French politicians, Frédéric Cournet and Emmanuel Barthélemy.
Prussia forbade duelling in 1851, and the ban was carried into the criminal code of the German Empire in 1871. The ritual student fencing of the Mensur survived in a non-lethal form.

In Russia, article 139 of Peter I's military code of 1715 provided that "all challenges, quarrels and duels are hereby most strictly forbidden", with hanging even where the duel ended without a wound. In a manifesto of 1787 Catherine II called duelling "a foreign implant" and imposed fines and exile to Siberia.

Pushkin died all the same, in a duel with Georges d'Anthès in 1837, and Lermontov in 1841, in a duel with a fellow officer, Nikolai Martynov. Then, under a law of 1894, the Russian army left the judgment whether a duel should be fought to a court of honour of the officer corps (the court of the society of officers). A ban had turned into a licence.

The last duel fought for honour in France was on 21 April 1967, at a private house in Neuilly-sur-Seine, where Gaston Defferre and René Ribière crossed swords. It began when Defferre called Ribière an imbecile on the floor of the National Assembly; Ribière was wounded twice and the seconds stopped the fight.

051.name: Foot binding (Chanzu)
051.hitokoto: The edict of 1902 did not forbid it. It said to urge gently.
body: Foot binding is held to have begun in the late Northern Song and to have spread as a custom under the Southern Song. Bound-foot remains have come out of the Southern Song tomb at Chayuanshan in Fuzhou, dated Chunyou 10, and the Zhou family tomb at De'an in Jiangxi, where the burial took place in Xianchun 10. The tomb of Huang Sheng in Fuzhou, found in 1975, held six pairs of women's shoes under 15 centimetres long and a cloth band 210 centimetres long. Tao Zongyi, writing at the turn of the Yuan and the Ming, set down in Chuogeng lu that before the Xining and Yuanfeng eras few women did it, while in recent years people copied one another and counted it a shame not to.

The Qing forbade it from Chongde 3 (1638), before they entered the passes. In Shunzhi 17 the husband or father of a woman who defied the edict was to receive eighty strokes of the rod and banishment of 3,000 li, and a further order came in Kangxi 3, but none was enforced in earnest. In early February 1902 the Empress Dowager Cixi held that the bound feet of Han women injured the harmony of creation, and directed that officials urge gently, so as to remove this accumulated habit by degrees. That is exhortation, not prohibition.

On 13 March 1912, Sun Yat-sen, provisional president, issued the Order of the Provisional President Instructing the Ministry of the Interior to Direct the Provinces to Urge the Prohibition of Foot Binding, in the Provisional Government Gazette no. 37. In Taiwan the household surveys of the Government-General showed the rate of bound feet falling from 56.94 per cent in 1905 to 17.36 per cent in 1915, and in that same year it became a formal prohibition in the baojia regulations. The last case confirmed on the mainland is from 1957.

made.label: Late Northern Song Origins
made.fact: Gao Hongxing's History of Foot Binding places its origin in the late Northern Song and its flourishing as a custom under the Southern Song. Archaeologically, bound-foot remains have come from the Southern Song tomb at Chayuanshan in Fuzhou, dated Chunyou 10 (1250), and from the Zhou family tomb at De'an in Jiangxi, buried in Xianchun 10 (1274). The tomb of Huang Sheng at Fucangshan in Fuzhou, found in October 1975 (she died in 1243, aged 16), yielded six pairs of women's shoes under 15 centimetres long and a cloth band 210 centimetres long and 9 centimetres wide.

discontinued.label: 1912 The order urging prohibition
discontinued.fact: On 13 March 1912, Sun Yat-sen, provisional president of the Republic of China, issued the Order of the Provisional President Instructing the Ministry of the Interior to Direct the Provinces to Urge the Prohibition of Foot Binding. It was published in the Provisional Government Gazette no. 37.

keyfacts.text: In the entry on foot binding in Chuogeng lu, Tao Zongyi, writing at the turn of the Yuan and the Ming, set down that "before the Xining and Yuanfeng eras there were still few who did it; in recent years people have copied one another, and count it a shame not to". This line fixes the point at which not doing it became shameful.

Before the Qing entered the passes, Emperor Taizong forbade women to "bind the hair and wrap the feet" in Chongde 3 (1638). In Shunzhi 17 the punishment set for a woman who bound her feet in defiance of the edict was eighty strokes of the rod and banishment of 3,000 li for her husband or father, and a further order was issued in Kangxi 3, but none was enforced in earnest. Manchu women never bound their feet at any time.

In early February 1902 the Empress Dowager Cixi issued an edict of exhortation against foot binding: "Han women mostly bind their feet, a thing long established, which injures the harmony of creation. You must urge them gently, so as to remove this accumulated habit by degrees." This was exhortation, not prohibition, and at the same time the ban on Manchu-Han intermarriage was relaxed.

In Taiwan, Huang Yujie and others founded the Taipei Natural Foot Society in 1900, and in the two household surveys of the Government-General, of 1905 and 1915, the rate of bound feet among women fell from 56.94 per cent to 17.36 per cent. Judging the new current settled, the Government-General made foot binding a formal prohibition in the baojia regulations of 1915.

In 1929 the Nationalist government issued a further Proclamation on Unbinding Feet and sent officers to supervise its enforcement. The Peking Chenbao of 1 February 1928 carried an article mocking the "foot-unbinding offices" of Henan and Shaanxi.

The last confirmed case of foot binding on the Chinese mainland is from 1957. Liuyi village in Tonghai county, Yunnan, is called "the last small-foot village in China" and still had 20 elderly women with bound feet as of 2017. The last small-shoe factory on the mainland, in Harbin, closed in November 1999.

052.name: Witch trials
052.hitokoto: In 1735 the law dropped witches and began punishing those who claimed to be one.
body: On 5 December 1484 Pope Innocent VIII issued a bull confirming to two Dominican inquisitors the power to try sorcery in five dioceses along the Rhine. Kramer, one of the two, got no cooperation locally, so he set out his own case in the Malleus Maleficarum and published it in 1487. The book went through 28 editions by 1600. Prosecutions in early modern Europe are estimated at about 100,000 and executions at 40,000 to 60,000.

What is worth noting is that this ended not in acquittal but in an exchange of defendant. The Witchcraft Act 1735 repealed the English act of 1604 and the Scottish act of 1563, and in their place punished anyone who pretended to practise witchcraft with a year's imprisonment and the pillory. The witch vanished from the world of the law, and the fraud who claimed to be one became the new defendant. The Act came into force on 24 June 1736.

Actual executions went on a little longer. On 13 June 1782 Anna Göldi was beheaded in the Swiss canton of Glarus. She is held to be the last person executed as a witch in Europe, though the charge in the judgment was not sorcery but poisoning. On 20 September 2007 the Swiss Federal Assembly accepted that the verdict had been wrong, and on 27 August 2008 the canton of Glarus cleared her name formally, as an unlawful trial. That was 226 years later.

made.label: 1484 A bull empowers the inquisitors
made.fact: On 5 December 1484, Pope Innocent VIII, in the bull Summis desiderantes affectibus, confirmed to the Dominican inquisitors Heinrich Kramer (Institoris) and Jakob Sprenger the power to try sorcery and heresy in the five dioceses of Mainz, Cologne, Trier, Salzburg and Bremen. Kramer obtained no cooperation locally and set out his own case in the Malleus Maleficarum (written in 1486, printed at Speyer in 1487).

discontinued.label: 1782 The last execution, in Glarus
discontinued.fact: On 13 June 1782, Anna Göldi was beheaded in the Swiss canton of Glarus. She is held to be the last person executed as a witch in Europe, though the charge in the judgment was not sorcery but poisoning (she was accused of putting needles into bread and milk by supernatural means). On 20 September 2007 the Swiss Federal Assembly accepted the verdict as wrong, and on 27 August 2008 the canton of Glarus formally cleared her name, calling it an "unlawful trial". That was 226 years later.

keyfacts.text: On 5 December 1484 the bull Summis desiderantes affectibus of Pope Innocent VIII confirmed to Kramer and Sprenger the power to try sorcery in five dioceses along the Rhine.

The Malleus Maleficarum was written in 1486 and printed at Speyer in 1487, and went through 28 editions between 1486 and 1600. The theology faculty of the University of Cologne, however, held its procedure unlawful and contrary to the demonology of the Church, and Kramer himself was condemned by the Inquisition in 1490. Because the papal bull was printed in the book's front matter, it was misread as carrying papal approval.

Prosecutions for sorcery in early modern Europe are estimated at about 100,000 and executions at 40,000 to 60,000. The peak runs from 1560 to 1630, with more than 40,000 deaths in that period alone. About 80 per cent of those convicted, and 75 to 85 per cent of those accused, were women.
The last executions by country were Jane Wenham in England (1712, later pardoned), Janet Horne in Scotland (1727), Maria Pauer in Austria (1750), and Anna Göldi in Switzerland (13 June 1782).

The Witchcraft Act 1735 (9 Geo. 2 c. 5) repealed the English act of 1604 (1 Jas. 1 c. 12) and the Scottish act of 1563, and in their place punished "pretending to exercise witchcraft" with a year's imprisonment without bail and an hour in the pillory each quarter in a market town. It came into force on 24 June 1736. The state struck the very existence of witches from the law and turned to punishing those who claimed to be one.
The canton of Glarus decided to clear Anna Göldi's name on 27 August 2008. The Swiss Federal Assembly had accepted the verdict as wrong the year before, on 20 September 2007.

053.name: The queue (Bianfa)
053.hitokoto: Not shaving meant death in 1645; not cutting broke the law in 1912. The same hairstyle.
body: The Qing, having entered the passes in 1644, forced the Manchu hairstyle on men, but resistance was strong and the order was withdrawn within a month. On the 29th day of the fifth month of Shunzhi 2 (1645) Dorgon issued the head-shaving order again, and on the 15th day of the sixth month it was proclaimed to soldiers and civilians throughout the country: whoever had not shaved within ten days of the order reaching him was to die. The words that have come down are "keep your head and lose your hair, keep your hair and lose your head".

For more than 260 years the queue remained a mark worn on the body to show submission to the dynasty. In Shunzhi 2 a descendant of Confucius petitioned to keep a dress code three thousand years old, and was stripped of office and barred from appointment for ever. On 6 May 1907 the Ministry of Education obtained approval for a strict ban on students and soldiers cutting the queue. The turn comes on 7 December 1911, when an edict, following a memorial from the Consultative Assembly, allowed subjects to cut their hair as they pleased.

On 5 March 1912, Sun Yat-sen, provisional president, promulgated the Order of the Provisional President Instructing the Ministry of the Interior to Notify the People to Cut the Queue Without Exception, in the Provisional Government Gazette no. 29: whoever had not yet parted with the queue had twenty days from the day the order reached him to cut it off completely, and those who did not comply would be dealt with as breaking the law. A hairstyle that kept a man alive if he shaved became unlawful if he did not cut it. Even so, in August 1916 the Ministry of the Interior was still ordering the cutting of hair to be pressed in Peking.

made.label: 1645 The head-shaving order
made.fact: On the 29th day of the fifth month of Shunzhi 2 (1645) Dorgon promulgated the head-shaving order again, and on the 15th day of the sixth month it was proclaimed to soldiers and civilians throughout the country, with death for whoever had not shaved within ten days of the order reaching him. The slogan "keep your head and lose your hair, keep your hair and lose your head" has come down from it. An order had also been issued immediately after the entry into the passes in 1644, but resistance was strong and it was withdrawn within a month.

discontinued.label: 1912 The order to cut the queue
discontinued.fact: On 5 March 1912, Sun Yat-sen, provisional president of the Republic of China, promulgated the Order of the Provisional President Instructing the Ministry of the Interior to Notify the People to Cut the Queue Without Exception: "all who have not removed the queue shall, within twenty days of the day this order reaches them, cut it off completely without exception; those who do not comply shall be held to have broken the law." It appeared in the Provisional Government Gazette no. 29.

keyfacts.text: The proclamation of the 15th day of the sixth month of Shunzhi 2 (1645) ordered the provinces to finish head-shaving within ten days of the order reaching them; those who broke it were to die, and local officials who memorialised against it were to be "killed without pardon". Inside and outside the capital the term was likewise ten days.

In the tenth month of Shunzhi 2, Kong Wenbiao, a descendant of Confucius and former circuit intendant of Hexi in Shaanxi, petitioned to be excepted and allowed to keep his hair, on the ground that "the dress code of my house has not been changed in three thousand years". Dorgon refused: "the head-shaving edict is strict, and those who break it are not pardoned… out of regard for the sage's line he is spared death. He is stripped of office and barred from appointment for ever." (Veritable Records of the Shunzhi Emperor)

On 6 May 1907 the central government of the Qing, on the approved memorial of the Ministry of Education, strictly forbade students and soldiers to cut the queue. A student found out was to be "reported to the Ministry of Education and punished according to his case", and soldiers, officers and men alike, were to be "dismissed at once".

On 7 December 1911 (17th day of the tenth lunar month), following a memorial from the Consultative Assembly, the Qing court issued an edict releasing the practice: "all Our subjects are permitted to cut their hair freely." The Shanghai Shishi xinbao reported it on 9 December 1911.

Some kept the queue even after the order of 5 March 1912, and on 21 August 1916 Sun Bolan, minister of the interior, ordered the district offices of Peking to "press on and cut them off strictly" (Shanghai Minguo ribao, 28 August 1916, "Hair to Be Cut Strictly").

In the same period, hairstyle was freed in Japan by Grand Council Proclamation No. 399 of 9 August Meiji 4 (23 September 1871) on cropped hair and the removal of swords, and in Korea a hair-cutting order was issued on 30 December 1895 (15th day of the eleventh lunar month), provoked strong resistance, and was withdrawn after the king's flight to the Russian legation.

054.name: Serfdom
054.hitokoto: A law was needed to forbid selling people without land. Which means it was normal.
body: Serfdom in Russia was not made at a stroke. The law code of 1497 confined a peasant's moving to the week either side of St George's Day; the code of 1550 raised the departure fee; the decrees of 1597 brought in forbidden years. The decisive step was the Sobornoye Ulozheniye of 1649, which abolished the time limit for pursuing a runaway peasant altogether. In 1658 flight itself became a criminal offence. A person became an appurtenance of the land.

Through the 18th and 19th centuries the landlord's power came close to unlimited. Ukrainian landlords were forbidden in 1798, and nobles who held no land in 1841, to sell serfs apart from land. That such laws were needed shows how common those sales were. In the census of 1857, 23.1 million out of 62.5 million people, 37.7 per cent, were privately held serfs.

On 19 February 1861 Alexander II issued the manifesto of emancipation. The land, however, had to be bought. The government advanced 75 per cent of the price to the landlord in bonds, and the peasants repaid it with interest over 49 years. In 1881 redemption was made compulsory, and the redemption payments went only in 1907. Serfs in Georgia were freed between 1864 and 1871, and serfdom among the Kalmyks lasted until 1892.

made.label: 1649 The code ends the time limit
made.fact: The Sobornoye Ulozheniye, the law code of 1649, tied peasants to the estate and abolished the time limit within which a runaway peasant could be pursued. In 1658 flight itself became a criminal offence. Before that, the law code (Sudebnik) of 1497 had confined the period for moving to the week either side of St George's Day, the code of 1550 raised the departure fee (pozhiloye), and the decrees of Boris Godunov in 1597 brought in "forbidden years", tightening the bond by stages.

discontinued.label: 1861 The emancipation manifesto
discontinued.fact: On 19 February 1861 (Old Style; 3 March New Style), Emperor Alexander II issued the manifesto of emancipation together with the Regulations concerning Peasants Leaving Serf Status. More than 23 million people were freed. In the census of 1857, privately held serfs numbered 23.1 million out of 62.5 million, 37.7 per cent of the population.

keyfacts.text: The law code of 1649 abolished the time limit for pursuing runaway peasants, and in 1658 flight became a criminal offence. In the censuses of 1678 and 1719, about four-fifths of Russian peasants were serfs.

Ukrainian landlords were forbidden in 1798, and nobles who held no land in 1841, to sell serfs apart from land. That such laws were needed is itself evidence that the sale of people without land was widely practised.
In the census of 1857, privately held serfs numbered 23.1 million out of 62.5 million, 37.7 per cent of the population.

Emancipation was not free. The government advanced 75 per cent of the price of the land to the landlord in bonds, and the peasants repaid the government with interest over 49 years. Those who could not buy the whole received a "pauper's allotment", a quarter of the arable, for nothing.

A decree of 1881 made redemption compulsory for the villages (mirs) that had not yet entered into it. In 1883, with arrears rising, repayments were cut by an average of 13 per cent, and the redemption payments themselves were abolished only in 1907, 46 years after emancipation.
The manifesto of 1861 excluded Georgia and the Kalmyks. The serfs of Georgia were freed between 1864 and 1871, and serfdom among the Kalmyks lasted until 1892.

055.name: Inquisition (Spanish)
055.hitokoto: The last person executed was a schoolteacher who taught his pupils deism. 1826.
body: On 1 November 1478 a bull of Pope Sixtus IV gave the Spanish crown the power to appoint inquisitors. The first auto de fe was held in Seville on 6 February 1481, where six people were burned alive. The tribunal did not burn people itself: it found them guilty and handed them to the secular power. Estimates of the number executed vary; Henry Kamen puts the toll for 1480 to 1530 at about 2,000.

It did not end once. The Chamartín decrees of Napoleon, of 4 December 1808, abolished the tribunal, and it was restored when Ferdinand VII returned. The final abolition came on 15 July 1834, by royal decree under the regency of María Cristina de Borbón. An institution of 356 years closed with a single decree.

The last person executed was Cayetano Ripoll, a schoolteacher in Valencia. He was put to death on 26 July 1826 for teaching his pupils deism and denying Catholic doctrine. The Church's tribunal of faith called for burning; the secular authorities chose hanging. That one case shows that the Church's sentence no longer bound the state.

made.label: 1478 A bull gives the crown a tribunal
made.fact: On 1 November 1478 the bull Exigit sincerae devotionis affectus of Pope Sixtus IV gave the Spanish crown the power to appoint inquisitors, and the Spanish Inquisition came into being. The first auto de fe (judgment of faith) was held in Seville on 6 February 1481, where six people were burned alive.

discontinued.label: 1834 Abolished by royal decree
discontinued.fact: On 15 July 1834, by royal decree under the regency of María Cristina de Borbón, the Spanish Inquisition was finally abolished throughout the kingdom. It coincides with the start of the reign of Isabella II. It had already been abolished once, by Napoleon's Chamartín decrees of 4 December 1808, but was revived when Ferdinand VII returned to the throne.

keyfacts.text: On 1 November 1478 a bull of Pope Sixtus IV brought the Spanish Inquisition into being. The first auto de fe was held in Seville on 6 February 1481, where six people were burned alive.
The last person executed by the Inquisition was Cayetano Ripoll, a schoolteacher in Valencia. He was executed on 26 July 1826 for teaching his pupils deism and denying Catholic doctrine.

In Ripoll's case the Church's tribunal of faith (junta de fe) called for burning, but the secular authorities chose hanging. The Church's sentence did not bind the state in law. After the execution his body is said to have been put into a barrel painted with flames and buried in unconsecrated ground.
On 4 December 1808 Napoleon's Chamartín decrees abolished the Inquisition once. It was revived when Ferdinand VII returned, and the matter was settled only by the royal decree of 15 July 1834.

Estimates of the number executed differ from scholar to scholar. Henry Kamen puts the executions of the fiercest period, 1480 to 1530, at about 2,000. On a wider reckoning, 3,000 to 5,000 are estimated to have been handed to the secular power in the first fifty years.

056.name: Index of Banned Books
056.hitokoto: The Church's list of what may not be read lost the force of law on 14 June 1966.
body: The first Roman Index, drawn up under the date of 30 December 1558 and published the following year, was the beginning of an international system for listing what the faithful might and might not read. In 1564 the Tridentine Index followed, on the authority of the Council of Trent. For 400 years after that the Index went through edition after edition, and its last, the twentieth, of 1948, listed about 4,000 titles.

The names on it show the reach of the system. Descartes, Galileo, Kant, Locke, Copernicus, Machiavelli, Voltaire, Rousseau. Nearly everyone who made modern philosophy and modern astronomy is there. It is also a record of how far the idea of deciding centrally what may be read was carried.

The end came with a notification of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith on 14 June 1966. The wording was careful: the Index no longer had the force of church law and the penalties were gone, but it was said to keep a moral force. The year before, Cardinal Ottaviani had answered in the negative when asked whether the Index would stay within the Congregation's competence. It was folded up quietly, in the period just after the Second Vatican Council.

made.label: 1559 The Roman Index
made.fact: The first Roman Index of Prohibited Books, the so-called Pauline Index, was made under Pope Paul IV. It is dated 30 December 1558 and was published in 1559. In 1564, on the authority of the Council of Trent, the Tridentine Index appeared under Pope Pius IV. For 400 years thereafter the Roman Curia maintained a system that listed the books the faithful were allowed to read.

discontinued.label: 1966 The notification of the Congregation
discontinued.fact: On 14 June 1966 a notification (Notificazione) of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith stated that the Index no longer had the force of church law. The penalties attached to it went as well, though the Index was said to retain a "moral force". In 1965 Cardinal Alfredo Ottaviani, asked whether the Index would remain within the Congregation's competence, had answered in the negative, so the abolition had been signalled in advance.

keyfacts.text: The first Roman Index was made under Pope Paul IV, dated 30 December 1558 and published in 1559. In 1564 the Tridentine Index followed on the authority of the Council of Trent.
The last edition was the twentieth, of 1948, which listed about 4,000 titles as subject to censorship, each with its reason.
The authors listed include Descartes, Galileo, Kant, Locke, Copernicus, Machiavelli, Voltaire and Rousseau. Nearly all the principal figures of modern philosophy and modern astronomy are there.

The notification of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith of 14 June 1966 stated that the Index "no longer has the force of church law". The Italian Wikipedia gives 15 November 1966 as the date the notification took effect.
In 1965 Cardinal Ottaviani, asked whether the Index would remain within the competence of the Congregation, answered in the negative. This was immediately after the Second Vatican Council.

057.name: Sacred Ground, No Women
057.hitokoto: 36 characters opened the sacred mountains in 1872. Mount Omine is closed still.
body: On 27 March Meiji 5 (4 May 1872) the Grand Council issued Proclamation No. 98: "Where places closed to women exist within the grounds of shrines and temples, they are abolished from now on, and climbing and worship there are left to one's pleasure." That is the whole text, 36 characters. It did not come out of a religious argument; what prompted it was the practical problem of foreign women being unable to enter the closed ground. The reasoning was that for a state trying to stand level with Europe and America such a custom was out of the question.

The exclusion itself is old. The pollution of childbirth blood was set down in the Konin shiki and that of menstruation in the Jogan shiki, and these are thought to have merged with the Buddhist precept against sexual conduct and the doctrine of the five obstructions of women to produce, by about the Kamakura period, the idea of a boundary closed to women. Indian Buddhism has no precept that bounds a place to exclude women, and Dogen wrote that Japan's boundary closed to women was "one of the laughable things in this country".

One proclamation was not the end of it. Mount Tate, Mount Haku and Mount Hiei opened in 1872, Mount Koya in 1904; women were first allowed to train as yamabushi on Mount Haguro in 1950. Sanjogatake on Mount Omine is closed to women over the whole mountain to this day. The sumo ring remained as well. In a statement from the chairman on 28 April 2018, the Japan Sumo Association said that an emergency is an exception and that award ceremonies are not.

made.label: Medieval The boundary takes shape
made.fact: The pollution of childbirth blood was set out in the Konin shiki (early 9th century), a supplementary code to the ritsuryo, and the pollution of menstruation in the Jogan shiki (late 9th century). This Shinto idea of pollution merged in the medieval period with the Buddhist precept against sexual conduct, the doctrine of the five obstructions of women and the doctrine of transformation into a male, and the notion of a boundary closed to women is thought to have taken shape around the Kamakura period, centred on the mountain temples and Shugendo. Indian Buddhism has no precept that bounds a place to forbid women's entry, and Dogen, in Shobogenzo, criticised the Japanese boundary closed to women as "one of the laughable things in this country".

discontinued.label: 1872 Grand Council Proclamation No. 98
discontinued.fact: Grand Council Proclamation No. 98 of 27 March Meiji 5 (4 May 1872). The whole text runs to 36 characters: "Where places closed to women exist within the grounds of shrines and temples, they are abolished from now on, and climbing and worship there are left to one's pleasure." It arose not from religious grounds but from the problem of foreign women being unable to enter ground closed to women, and it was forbidden as a "base custom" out of the question for a modern state ranking with Europe and America.

keyfacts.text: Grand Council Proclamation No. 98 runs to 36 characters in all: "Where places closed to women exist within the grounds of shrines and temples, they are abolished from now on, and climbing and worship there are left to one's pleasure." The original is published in the National Diet Library Digital Collections, pid/994264.

The opening was not simultaneous. Mount Tate, Mount Haku and Mount Hiei in 1872, Mount Ontake around 1877, Mount Koya in 1904. Mount Gassan and Mount Yudono of the Three Mountains of Dewa were opened in 1877, but women were first allowed to train as yamabushi on Mount Haguro only in 1950.

Sanjogatake on Mount Omine in Nara Prefecture kept the exclusion as a rule of the order after the proclamation, and the whole mountain is closed to women to this day, with signs standing on the paths. Three proposals to open it, at the designation of the national park in 1936, from the temple side in 1997, and in the 1,300th memorial year of En no Gyoja in 2000, all came to nothing.

The ring in professional sumo is still closed to women. At an extraordinary meeting of the board on 28 April 2018, and in a statement from the chairman the same day, the Japan Sumo Association held that a woman may enter the ring as an exception in an emergency, but that ceremonies such as the presentation of prizes are not to be treated as exceptions (House of Councillors Committee on Education, Culture and Science, 29 May 2018).

Fusae Ota, the first woman governor in Japan, for eight years from 2000, said herself, in the House of Councillors Committee on Education, Culture and Science on 29 May 2018, that she had asked the association whether she could enter the ring to hand the Osaka prefectural governor's prize to the champion in person at the Osaka tournament.

The exclusion of women from festivals is thought to have been taken up only in the Edo period or the Meiji period and after, and the Kojiki describes women taking part in festivals. In the utaki of Okinawa the reverse holds: men are excluded there to this day.

058.name: Yangban
058.hitokoto: The line between yangban and commoner left the law with a single resolution, in 1894.
body: Status in the Joseon dynasty divided into yangban, jungin, commoners and slaves, and the frame was set by the Gyeongguk daejeon, promulgated in 1470 and settled in 1485. The road into office was the examination, and a man who passed and was allowed the black hat took yangban status. Yangban are put at about 3 per cent of the population early in the dynasty, but towards its end status could be bought with money, and in some districts more than 70 per cent of households were yangban on the register.

The resolutions of the Deliberative Council, set up on 27 July 1894, held yangban and commoners equal in law, provided that talent be appointed regardless of high or low birth and family line, that the documents of public and private slaves be done away with and the trade in persons forbidden, and that the examination system be abolished and a new method of appointing officials laid down. Widows were allowed to remarry, early marriage was forbidden, and guilt by association and torture in punishment were abolished.

On 7 January 1895, King Gojong and the crown prince led the civil and military officials to the royal ancestral shrine and swore the Fourteen Articles before the spirits of their ancestors. The fourteenth reads: in employing men, do not ask after family line, but appoint talent widely. The Korean examinations ended at the same time. China's would stop eleven years later. It has been argued, though, that many of the resolutions were never put into effect at all and became dead letters.

made.label: Late 15th c. The Gyeongguk daejeon
made.fact: The status order of the Joseon dynasty was framed by the Gyeongguk daejeon, the law code whose compilation began in the reign of King Sejo, which was promulgated in 1470 (Seongjong 1) and finally settled in 1485 (Seongjong 16). The road into office was the examination, and men who passed it took yangban status.

discontinued.label: 1894 The Council resolutions
discontinued.fact: The resolutions of the Deliberative Council (Gungungimucheo), set up on 27 July 1894, laid down that yangban and commoners were equal in law and that talent be appointed regardless of high or low birth and family line, that the documents of public and private slaves be abolished and the trade in persons forbidden, and that the examination system be abolished. On 7 January 1895 (12th day of the twelfth lunar month of 1894), King Gojong and the crown prince led the civil and military officials to the royal ancestral shrine and swore the Fourteen Articles (Hongbeom 14jo) before the spirits of their ancestors. The fourteenth article: "In employing men, family line shall not be considered, and talent shall be appointed widely."

keyfacts.text: The resolutions of the Deliberative Council include equality in law between yangban and commoners, abolition of the discrimination that put civil office above military, destruction of the documents of public and private slaves and prohibition of the trade in persons, prohibition of early marriage (men 20 and over, women 16 and over), permission for widows to remarry, abolition of guilt by association and of torture in punishment, and abolition of the examination system. Until a new criminal code was made, the Daejeon hoetong (1865) was to remain in force.

The resolutions of the Deliberative Council are recorded in the Veritable Records of King Gojong, book 31, under Gojong 31, sixth month, 28th day (gyeyu): "the Deliberative Council submits resolutions abolishing guilt by association, breaking down family lines, abolishing the status system and so on" (vol. 35, book 31, leaf 39 recto).

The Second Gabo Reform (17 December 1894 to 6 July 1895, the coalition cabinet of Kim Hong-jip and Pak Yong-hyo) "abolished the distinction between civil and military and between yangban and commoner by reforming the status system". The administrative divisions were also recast from 8 provinces into 23 prefectures and 337 counties.

Yangban are said to have been only about 3 per cent of the population early in the Joseon dynasty, but towards the end of it yangban status could be bought with money without sitting the examination, and in some districts more than 70 per cent of households were yangban on the register. It has been argued that the growing number of tax-exempt people brought on fiscal trouble and was one cause of the abolition of the status system.

The Fourteen Articles are regarded as the first law of constitutional character in Korea. The Gabo Reform, however, was carried through under Japanese pressure, and many of the resolutions of the Deliberative Council were never begun and became dead letters.
The examinations were abolished by the same resolutions that abolished the status system. China's examinations stopped eleven years later, on 2 September 1905.

059.name: Primogeniture
059.hitokoto: The rule giving the eldest son all the land was abolished on 1 January 1926.
body: At common law in England, freehold land descended to the eldest son alone. Local customs survived here and there: partible inheritance under the gavelkind of Kent, inheritance by the youngest son under borough English. Where land went was settled by order of birth. The whole arrangement disappeared in a single provision: section 45(1) of the Administration of Estates Act 1925.

Section 45(1) states that it abolishes all existing modes, rules and canons of descent. Local customs, the husband's curtesy, the wife's dower, and escheat to the Crown where there was no heir were all covered together. Section 58(2) set the commencement at 1 January 1926. Section 45(2), however, excluded entailed interests, so succession to an estate could still be kept up by settlement.

Inheritance among private persons changed; the Crown did not. Male-preference primogeniture lasted until section 1 of the Succession to the Crown Act 2013, and that section reaches only those born after 28 October 2011. It came into force on 26 March 2015. A principle that ended for land in 1926 ended for the Crown 89 years later.

made.label: Medieval common law The canons of descent
made.fact: At common law in England, freehold land followed the canons of descent, by which the eldest son inherited alone. Local customs survived as exceptions in various places, such as the gavelkind of Kent (partible inheritance) and borough English (inheritance by the youngest son). That section 45 of the Administration of Estates Act 1925 abolished "all existing modes, rules and canons of descent" is itself evidence that they were alive until then.

discontinued.label: 1925 Administration of Estates Act s.45
discontinued.fact: Section 45(1) of the Administration of Estates Act 1925 (15 & 16 Geo. 5 c. 23) abolished, as to the real estate and personal inheritance of anyone dying after the commencement of the Act, (a) all existing modes, rules and canons of descent (including local customs such as gavelkind and borough English), (b) curtesy, the husband's right, (c) dower and freebench, the wife's right, and (d) escheat to the Crown, the Duchy of Lancaster or the Duke of Cornwall for want of heirs. Section 58(2) provides that "this Act shall come into operation on the first day of January nineteen hundred and twenty-six". It extends to England and Wales.

keyfacts.text: Section 45(1) of the Administration of Estates Act 1925 abolished, together, the modes, rules and canons of descent, curtesy, dower and escheat. Local customs such as gavelkind and borough English went at the same time.

Section 58(2) of the same Act provides that "this Act shall come into operation on the first day of January nineteen hundred and twenty-six", and section 58(3) confines its application to England and Wales.

Section 45(2), however, reserved that "nothing in this section affects the descent or devolution of an entailed interest". The frame of succession to an estate, gone from intestate inheritance, was left in the form of an entail created by settlement.

Section 46 of the Act brought into one the order of intestate succession, which had differed between real estate and personal estate. Section 45 removed the old order and section 46 put the new one in its place: two steps.

In succession to the Crown, male-preference primogeniture lasted until section 1 of the Succession to the Crown Act 2013 (2013 c. 20), which provides that "in determining the succession to the Crown, the gender of a person born after 28 October 2011 does not give that person, or that person's descendants, precedence over any other person (whenever born)". It came into force on 26 March 2015 (S.I. 2015/894, article 2).

060.name: Same-Clan Marriage Ban
060.hitokoto: The rule against marrying anyone of the same surname and origin died on 1 January 1999.
body: Marriage between people of the same surname and the same ancestral seat was forbidden from the beginning of the Joseon period, when the new scholar-officials brought in Neo-Confucianism, and it was recognised as Korean customary law under Japanese rule as well. In the Republic of Korea, article 809(1) of the Civil Act, promulgated on 22 February 1958 and in force from 1 January 1960, provided that blood relatives of the same surname and origin could not marry. A marriage in breach of it could be annulled on the application of collateral blood relatives within the eighth degree.

In China the ban on marriage between people of the same surname was abolished on 5 May 1931, when the book on relatives of the Civil Code of the Republic of China came into force; in North Korea it was abolished in 1948. In Korea objection continued to forbidding, on surname and ancestral seat alone, a range far too wide for any blood tie to be shown, and a Special Act on Marriage was put in place for one year each in 1978, 1988 and 1996, so that couples living as married could register.

On 16 July 1997 the Constitutional Court, in the joined cases 95 Hun-Ka 6 to 13, held the article incompatible with the Constitution and ruled that it would lose its force on 1 January 1999 if the legislature had not amended it by 31 December 1998. No amendment was made, and the article lapsed. The formal deletion came by Act No. 7427 of 31 March 2005, and the criterion now is blood relationship within the eighth degree.

made.label: Early Joseon Neo-Confucianism arrives
made.fact: Marriage between persons of the same surname and the same ancestral seat was forbidden from the beginning of the Joseon period, when the new scholar-officials brought in Neo-Confucianism, and it was recognised as Korean customary law under Japanese rule. It was put into modern statute as article 809(1) of the Civil Act (Act No. 471), promulgated on 22 February 1958 and in force from 1 January 1960: "Blood relatives of the same surname and origin may not marry."

discontinued.label: 1999 The article loses its force
discontinued.fact: On 16 July 1997 the Constitutional Court, in 95 Hun-Ka 6 to 13 (joined), held article 809(1) of the Civil Act incompatible with the Constitution and ruled that "the above provision shall lose its force on 1 January 1999 if the legislature has not amended it by 31 December 1998". The legislature did not amend it in time, and the article lost its force on 1 January 1999. The formal deletion came by Act No. 7427 of 31 March 2005.

keyfacts.text: Article 809 of the Civil Act (Act No. 471, enacted 22 February 1958, in force 1 January 1960) provided: "(Prohibition of marriage between persons of the same surname and origin, and the like) (1) Blood relatives of the same surname and origin may not marry." Under article 817, a marriage in breach of it could be annulled on the application of the parties, their lineal ascendants, or collateral blood relatives within the eighth degree.

In China the ban on marriage between persons of the same surname was abolished on 5 May 1931, when the book on relatives of the Civil Code of the Republic of China came into force; in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea the ban on marriage between persons of the same surname and origin was abolished in 1948. Even when the Korean Civil Act was enacted, there were objections that it was "anachronistic legislation".

Objection continued to forbidding, on surname and ancestral seat alone, a range too wide for any blood tie to be shown, and a Special Act on Marriage was in force for one year each in 1978, 1988 and 1996, allowing couples of the same surname and origin who were living as married to register their marriage.

The decision of the Constitutional Court of 16 July 1997 also ordered that application be suspended: "the courts and other state organs and local governments shall suspend the application of the above provision until the legislature amends it."

On 2 March 2005 the National Assembly passed a bill amending the Civil Act, and by Act No. 7427, promulgated on 31 March, article 809 was changed to read "(Prohibition of marriage between close relatives and the like) (1) Blood relatives within the eighth degree … may not marry." Prohibition by surname and ancestral seat was replaced by a criterion of blood relationship within the eighth degree.

Act No. 7427, promulgated the same day, 31 March 2005, also abolished the head-of-household system (that abolition taking effect on 1 January 2008). The deletion of the ban on marriage between persons of the same surname and origin differed in that it took effect on promulgation.

061.name: Suicide as a crime
061.hitokoto: In 1823 a statute was needed to forbid burying a suicide with a stake through the body.
body: At common law in England, suicide was felo de se, a felony against oneself. Because it was a crime, the treatment of the body was part of the punishment. The Burial of Suicide Act 1823 forbade burial in a highway or at a crossroads and the driving of a stake through the body. That a statute was needed to forbid it shows that it was being done. It received royal assent on 8 July 1823.

What the Act of 1823 removed was only the place and the stake. Burial was still required within 24 hours of the close of the inquest, between 9 p.m. and midnight, and without Christian rites. Those restrictions went only with the Interments (felo de se) Act 1882, in force from 3 July 1882. It took 59 years for the dead to be treated ordinarily.

The crime itself went in 1961. Section 1 of the Suicide Act is a single sentence: "The rule of law whereby it is a crime for a person to commit suicide is hereby abrogated." It is short because what it abolished was not a statute but a rule of the common law. Section 2, however, kept the encouraging and assisting of another's suicide a crime, with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

made.label: Medieval common law A felony against oneself
made.fact: At common law in England, suicide was felo de se, a felony against oneself. Section 1 of the Suicide Act 1961 provides that "the rule of law whereby it is a crime for a person to commit suicide is hereby abrogated", and that provision is itself evidence that suicide had remained a crime until then. Until 1823 the law took for granted the burial of a suicide in a highway or at a crossroads with a stake driven through the body.

discontinued.label: 1961 Suicide Act s.1
discontinued.fact: Section 1 of the Suicide Act 1961 (9 & 10 Eliz. 2 c. 60) is a single sentence: "The rule of law whereby it is a crime for a person to commit suicide is hereby abrogated." It extends to England and Wales. Section 2, however, kept the aiding and abetting of another's suicide a crime, punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment (the present wording of section 2 is that of later amendments).

keyfacts.text: Section 1 of the Suicide Act 1961 is one sentence in full: "The rule of law whereby it is a crime for a person to commit suicide is hereby abrogated." It extends to England and Wales.

Section 2 of the same Act kept as a crime the encouraging of, or assisting in, another's suicide or attempted suicide, with up to 14 years' imprisonment on indictment. Suicide was decriminalised, but taking part in one remained a crime.

The full title of the Burial of Suicide Act 1823 (4 Geo. 4 c. 52, royal assent 8 July 1823) is "An Act to alter and amend the Law relating to the Interment of the Remains of any Person found Felo de se". It forbade burial in a highway and the driving of a stake through the body. Which is to say that until 1823 this was being done.

All the Act of 1823 forbade was the place and the stake; it went on requiring burial within 24 hours of the close of the inquest, between 9 p.m. and midnight, and without Christian rites. Those restrictions went only with the Interments (felo de se) Act 1882, in force from 3 July 1882.

The decriminalisation of suicide (1961), the abolition of the duty of rite-less burial at night (1882), and the prohibition of highway burial and the stake (1823) are all different statutes with different dates. This was not something settled at one stroke.
